title: Making a browser game with Claude Code: the workflow, the real test, the PAIN
author: SvitsGames
selftext:
**Play it free in your browser, no sign-up. There are two versions:**

* **The original, harder one** (itch.io, no ads): [https://svitsgames.itch.io/edgy-fox](https://svitsgames.itch.io/edgy-fox)
* **An easier one** (Playgama, with ads): [https://playgama.ai/play/ihafoukuma](https://playgama.ai/play/ihafoukuma)

I've spent about two months building Edgy Fox with Claude Code. The whole level is the edge of your screen: the fox runs around it by itself, and you get two moves, tap to jump and hold to stop. Boars and deer bounce around the middle, hares and birds come at you along the edge, and every season ends with a boss. A death ends the run, but your coins and upgrades stay. After winter, a new year starts, a little harder, with a twist of its own. It works on a phone or a PC, in portrait or landscape, with touch, mouse, keyboard, or gamepad.

The two versions are the part I most want to talk about, because they came straight out of the AI workflow. More on that below.

# How the work was split

I'm a web developer with 15+ years of experience, and I've been playing video games for 30+ years, from Tetris and the NES to modern triple-A titles. Universe, I love video games, they're my favorite form of media. So I came up with the gameplay, made the design calls, wrote the rules Claude works by, reviewed its changes, and played every build on my phone, my PC, and with a gamepad. When something felt off, it went back to Claude. Claude did most of the typing: about 530 of the \~600 commits are co-authored by it. I do, however, understand every line of code, unfortunately for me.

The models are Claude Opus 5 and then Opus 5.5 in the main session and Sonnet 5.5 for two subagents.

# The setup that kept it on track

The thing that mattered most was keeping decisions in files instead of in the chat. There's a short CLAUDE.md plus 15 rule files (design, layout, assets, licensing, the portal and so on), and each one loads only when Claude opens a file it covers, so the context stays small. Every decision goes in with a date and a reason. That way, when a new session wants to "improve" something we already settled, the reason is right there, and we don't argue about the same thing twice. Most of the time.

The second thing was keeping the game's rules apart from the engine. All the logic is plain TypeScript with no Phaser in it, so 610 checks run the real game code in Node in a few seconds, no browser. Claude runs them after every change, and it has to back every claim with a file and a line number or a command's output. "The tests pass" only counts when the output says so.

Then there are balance bots that play the real game in headless Chromium. My first bots had perfect reflexes, so I tuned the game against a machine and it came out way too hard. Now they react 220 to 380 ms late with sloppy taps, more like a thumb on a phone. Still, a bot isn't a player.

Smaller pieces: two subagents (one writes code from a plan we already agreed on, the other checks a build against the portal's requirements; most changes are quicker in the main session, so I only use them when it's worth it) and two skills (one cuts a release: size limits, where every asset came from, license notices, the zip; the other runs a difficulty pass after I play on a device). Never put special characters in your zip file names, and a dot counts as one. I rediscover this every time I make that stupid mistake.

# Letting Claude read the player data

The game went to Playgama's sandbox first, and Playgama has an MCP server, so Claude can upload builds, set up leaderboards and read the player telemetry itself. That turned into a loop: Claude reads the numbers, we look for where people drop off, I decide what to change, Claude builds it, and the next build gets measured again. Most updates since launch came out of it:

* Most new players quit during the tutorial or at their first death. The tutorial got shorter, and new players can't lose a run in the first season (spring) before its boss.
* A third of them got stuck on "hold to stop", because holding the left mouse button jumped. Now it stops, like holding a finger on a phone.
* Players who left early hadn't pressed anything yet, because the first thing to jump over came about 5 seconds in. Now it comes in 2.
* Some players just sat there when the tutorial said "hold to stop". Now the tutorial never waits on you: if you don't do the move within a few seconds, it does it for you and carries on. It also uses fewer words, and the first boss shows up about 45 seconds into the run after it.

# Why there are two versions

Following the data also meant easing the game: the speed ramps up more slowly, there are fewer animals, and spring is hard to lose. That's the Playgama version. The original was a lot harder, and honestly I liked it that way, but the casual browser players didn't agree. So the original went up on itch.io: the speed climbs 50% faster, summer and winter have more animals, and after the first year every season gets winter's lineup plus an extra boar.

Code-wise, both are branches of one core, and every fix lands in the core first, then goes out to each branch. Claude handles the merges, and the rule files say which values each branch keeps on a conflict.

This is the part I keep thinking about. When an agent reads the telemetry for you, every suggestion pushes the game toward the player who quits first. That's useful, but if you follow it all the way, you end up with a different game. Keeping both was my way of not choosing.

# Tools and assets

* Phaser 4.1 (the game engine), TypeScript, and Vite
* Playwright: the bots in headless Chromium, plus a WebKit smoke test for Safari-like browsers
* Python with Pillow and ffmpeg: the asset pipeline that cuts, recolors, and compresses the art and audio (Claude wrote the script)
* Playgama Bridge SDK on the Playgama version: saves, ads, leaderboards, and achievements

The art and audio aren't generated. They're ready-made packs: Craftpix pixel art, Kenney's sounds, four pizzicato tracks by Sonican from Pixabay, and the Jersey 10 font. So the AI side of this project is the code, the workflow, and reading the data. The fox's 22 colors are all recolors of one sprite sheet.

# What I liked and didn't

Making small games with Claude Code is a lot of fun. It's like pair programming with a very fast typist who can also read the docs and check the code. I have to review what it writes (ok, let's be honest, maybe not every line, but at least every function or logical part), and it's not perfect, but it's very good at following rules and keeping the code clean once the rules are written down.

What I didn't like was nerfing the game for casual browser players. The metrics answered fast: most of them quit in the tutorial (lol). It's a good lesson for me, and it's why the original lives on itch now.

# Questions for you

* If you let an agent read your game's analytics, how do you stop it from sanding the game down to whatever keeps the first-minute players?
* How do you keep design decisions from drifting between sessions? Rule files with dates work for me, but I'd love to hear other setups.

And if you give the game a go, tell me which version you played, where you stopped, and whether it felt too hard or too easy. Thanks!

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body: Shipping two difficulty versions on two platforms is a smart way to learn what actually keeps people playing. The browser lesson that surprised me most on Hatched (a city where every resident is an AI) was about placement, not content: when talking to your citizen lived in a side panel, almost nobody did it, and putting it on the main screen with one-tap opening lines did more than any model change. Which version is holding players longer so far, the hard one or the easy one?

replies.author: SvitsGames
replies.body: The easy one for sure, which is not surprising (but it makes me sad a bit).
